## Ring Homomorphisms

A ring homomorphism $\phi:R\to S$ preserves addition and multiplication:

$$
\phi(a+b)=\phi(a)+\phi(b), \qquad
\phi(ab)=\phi(a)\phi(b).
$$

If $\phi$ is one-to-one and onto, it is an **isomorphism** of rings.

## Example: Reduction Modulo $n$

Define $\phi:\mathbb{Z}\to\mathbb{Z}_n$ by $\phi(a)=[a]$.

This map preserves addition and multiplication modulo $n$. Its kernel is

$$
\ker\phi=\{a\in\mathbb{Z}:\phi(a)=[0]\}=n\mathbb{Z}.
$$

So the integers that map to zero are exactly the multiples of $n$.

## Ideals

An **ideal** $I$ of a ring $R$ is a subring that satisfies: if $a\in I$ and $r\in R$, then $ra$ and $ar$ belong to $I$.

Trivial Examples: Every ring has the trivial ideals $\{0\}$ and $R$.

In a commutative ring with identity, the ideal generated by as single element $a$ is $\langle a\rangle=\{ar:r\in R\}.$ If an ideal is generate by a single element is called a **principal ideal**.

## Every Ideal of $\mathbb{Z}$ Is Principal

Let $I$ be a nonzero ideal of $\mathbb{Z}$. Choose its least positive element $n$.

For any $a\in I$, the division algorithm gives $a=nq+r$, where $0\le r<n$.

Since $r=a-nq$ belongs to $I$, minimality of $n$ forces $r=0$. Thus every $a\in I$ is a multiple of $n$, and

$$
I=n\mathbb{Z}=\langle n\rangle.
$$



## Principal Ideal Domains

An **integral domain** in which every ideal is principal is called a **principal ideal domain (PID)**.

For example, $\mathbb{Z}$ and $\mathbb{Q}[x]$ are PIDs. But $\mathbb{Q}[x,y]$ is not: the ideal $(x,y)$ is not principal. 

## Kernels Are Ideals

For a ring homomorphism $\phi:R\to S$, its kernel is

$$
\ker\phi=\{a\in R:\phi(a)=0\}.
$$

It is an additive subgroup. If $a\in\ker\phi$ and $r\in R$, then

$$
\phi(ar)=\phi(a)\phi(r)=0
\quad\text{and}\quad
\phi(ra)=\phi(r)\phi(a)=0.
$$

Therefore, $\ker\phi$ is an ideal of $R$.

## Quotient Rings

If $I$ is an ideal of $R$, the cosets of $I$ form a quotient ring $R/I$.

Addition is the usual coset addition, and multiplication is defined by

$$
(r+I)(s+I)=rs+I.
$$

The ideal property ensures that this product does not depend on which representatives of the cosets are chosen.

## The Natural Map

For an ideal $I$ of $R$, define $\phi:R\to R/I$ by

$$
\phi(r)=r+I.
$$

This map is onto, and its kernel is $I$.

Thus the ideal used to form the quotient is exactly the set of elements sent to zero by the natural map.

## First Isomorphism Theorem

If $\psi:R\to S$ is a ring homomorphism, then

$$
R/\ker\psi \cong \psi(R).
$$

The quotient by the kernel captures the image of the homomorphism: elements that map to the same value are identified in the quotient.

## Connections to Ring Types

| Idea | Connection |
|:---|:---|
| Kernel  | ß ideal |
| Quotient by an ideal | Forms a quotient ring |
| Prime ideal $P$ | $R/P$ is an integral domain |
| Maximal ideal $M$ | $R/M$ is a field |
| Integral domain | Cancellation holds: if $a\ne 0$ and $ab=ac$, then $b=c$ |
| Euclidean domain | The Euclidean algorithm finds greatest common divisors  |

For commutative rings with identity,

$$
\text{field} \Longrightarrow \text{Euclidean domain}
\Longrightarrow \text{integral domain}.
$$
